title: Deep Learning Fundamentals and Backpropagation
summary: Backpropagation is the algorithm that makes deep learning possible - it efficiently computes how much each weight contributed to the error using the chain rule, then updates weights to reduce loss. Beyond the core algorithm, practical training relies
content:
# Deep Learning Fundamentals and Backpropagation ##### The 24-hour training run that learned nothing An engineer left a network training overnight on a rented GPU. Twelve hours in, they checked the logs: loss stuck at 0.693 from epoch 3 onwards, flat as a table. 0.693 is `ln(2)`. It is exactly the binary cross-entropy of a model outputting 0.5 for every input — the loss of a coin flip. The network had stopped learning almost immediately and spent eleven hours confirming it. The cause was a sigmoid activation in every hidden layer of a six-layer network. Sigmoid's derivative maxes out at 0.25, so gradients passing back through six layers were multiplied by at most `0.25⁶ ≈ 0.00024`. By the time the signal reached the early layers it was effectively zero, and those layers never updated. This is the **vanishing gradient problem**, and it is one of several failure modes that separate "the code runs" from "the model learns." Understanding backpropagation and the machinery around it is what lets you read a flat loss curve and know why. ##### Backpropagation Backpropagation computes how much each weight contributed to the error, using the chain rule applied backwards through the network. The insight that makes it efficient: computing gradients naively — perturbing each weight and re-running the forward pass — would cost one forward pass per parameter. For a million parameters that is a million forward passes per step. Backpropagation computes **all** gradients in a single backward pass, reusing intermediate results (Rumelhart, Hinton & Williams, 1986). The mechanics, for a two-layer network: ```text Forward: z1 = XW₁ + b₁ → a1 = relu(z1) → z2 = a1W₂ + b₂ → ŷ = sigmoid(z2) Backward: ∂L/∂ŷ → ∂L/∂z2 → ∂L/∂W₂, ∂L/∂b₂, ∂L/∂a1 → ∂L/∂z1 → ∂L/∂W₁, ∂L/∂b₁ ``` ```python import numpy as np class Network: def __init__(self, n_in, n_hidden, n_out, seed=42): rng = np.random.default_rng(seed) self.W1 = rng.normal(0, np.sqrt(2 / n_in), (n_in, n_hidden)) self.b1 = np.zeros(n_hidden) self.W2 = rng.normal(0, np.sqrt(2 / n_hidden), (n_hidden, n_out)) self.b2 = np.zeros(n_out) def forward(self, X): self.X = X self.z1 = X @ self.W1 + self.b1 self.a1 = np.maximum(0, self.z1) # ReLU self.z2 = self.a1 @ self.W2 + self.b2 self.out = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-np.clip(self.z2, -500, 500))) return self.out def backward(self, y): m = y.shape[0] # Sigmoid + BCE combine to this elegantly simple form dz2 = (self.out - y) / m # (batch, n_out) dW2 = self.a1.T @ dz2 # (n_hidden, n_out) db2 = dz2.sum(axis=0) da1 = dz2 @ self.W2.T # propagate back dz1 = da1 * (self.z1 > 0) # ReLU derivative: 1 or 0 dW1 = self.X.T @ dz1 db1 = dz1.sum(axis=0) return {"W1": dW1, "b1": db1, "W2": dW2, "b2": db2} ``` Two things to notice. `dz2 = (out - y) / m` is remarkably simple — sigmoid's derivative and cross-entropy's derivative cancel almost entirely, which is one reason that pairing is standard. And `dz1 = da1 * (self.z1 > 0)` is ReLU's derivative: gradient passes through where the input was positive, and is blocked where it was not. **Gradient checking** verifies your implementation numerically, and is worth doing once: ```python def gradient_check(net, X, y, param="W1", eps=1e-5): """Compare analytic gradients against numerical ones.""" net.forward(X); grads = net.backward(y) W = getattr(net, param) i, j = 0, 0 W[i, j] += eps loss_plus = bce(y, net.forward(X)) W[i, j] -= 2 * eps loss_minus = bce(y, net.forward(X)) W[i, j] += eps # restore numerical = (loss_plus - loss_minus) / (2 * eps) print(f"analytic {grads[param][i, j]:.8f} numerical {numerical:.8f}") ``` If those two numbers disagree beyond about `1e-6`, your backward pass has a bug. ##### Optimizers The plain update rule — `θ ← θ − α∇L` — is **stochastic gradient descent**. It works, but it struggles in ravines (steep in one direction, shallow in another) and gets stuck on plateaus. **Momentum** accumulates a velocity, carrying the update through flat regions and damping oscillations: ```python class SGDMomentum: def __init__(self, params, lr=0.01, momentum=0.9): self.lr, self.momentum = lr, momentum self.velocity = {k: np.zeros_like(v) for k, v in params.items()} def step(self, params, grads): for k in params: self.velocity[k] = self.momentum * self.velocity[k] - self.lr * grads[k] params[k] += self.velocity[k] ``` **Adam** (Kingma & Ba, 2014) combines momentum with **per-parameter adaptive learning rates**, scaling each step by a running estimate of that parameter's gradient magnitude: ```python class Adam: def __init__(self, params, lr=0.001, beta1=0.9, beta2=0.999, eps=1e-8): self.lr, self.b1, self.b2, self.eps = lr, beta1, beta2, eps self.m = {k: np.zeros_like(v) for k, v in params.items()} # 1st moment self.v = {k: np.zeros_like(v) for k, v in params.items()} # 2nd moment self.t = 0 def step(self, params, grads): self.t += 1 for k in params: self.m[k] = self.b1 * self.m[k] + (1 - self.b1) * grads[k] self.v[k] = self.b2 * self.v[k] + (1 - self.b2) * grads[k] ** 2 m_hat = self.m[k] / (1 - self.b1 ** self.t) # bias correction v_hat = self.v[k] / (1 - self.b2 ** self.t) params[k] -= self.lr * m_hat / (np.sqrt(v_hat) + self.eps) ``` | Optimizer | Typical LR | Strengths | Weaknesses | |---|---|---|---| | **SGD** | 0.01–0.1 | Simple, generalizes well | Slow, LR-sensitive | | **SGD + momentum** | 0.01–0.1 | Faster, escapes plateaus | Still needs LR tuning | | **Adam** | **0.001** | Fast, robust default | Can generalize slightly worse | | **AdamW** | 0.001 | Adam with correct weight decay | — | **Use Adam with `lr=0.001` as your default.** It works acceptably on almost anything with no tuning. For state-of-the-art results in vision, SGD with momentum and a good schedule often edges ahead — but start with Adam. The `eps` in the denominator prevents division by zero, and the bias correction matters in early steps when the moment estimates are still near zero. ##### Vanishing and exploding gradients The problem from the opening story, stated precisely. Backpropagation multiplies derivatives layer by layer. If each is less than 1, the product shrinks exponentially with depth — **vanishing gradients**, and early layers stop learning. If each exceeds 1, the product explodes and weights become `NaN`. ```python depth = 10 sigmoid_max_deriv = 0.25 print(f"Sigmoid, {depth} layers: {sigmoid_max_deriv ** depth:.2e}") # 9.54e-07 print(f"ReLU, {depth} layers: {1.0 ** depth:.2e}") # 1.00e+00 ``` The mitigations, and the assignment asks for two: **1. ReLU activations.** Derivative is exactly 1 for positive inputs, so gradients pass through undiminished. This single change is the largest factor in making deep networks trainable and it is why ReLU replaced sigmoid in hidden layers. **2. Careful initialization.** He initialization for ReLU (`√(2/n_in)`) and Xavier for tanh (`√(1/n_in)`) keep activation variance stable across layers so gradients neither shrink nor grow systematically. **3. Batch normalization** — covered below — normalizes each layer's inputs, keeping them in the range where gradients flow well. **4. Residual (skip) connections** — `output = F(x) + x` — give gradients a direct path backwards that bypasses the layer entirely. This is what enables networks hundreds of layers deep. **5. Gradient clipping** for the exploding case: ```python def clip_gradients(grads, max_norm=1.0): total = np.sqrt(sum(np.sum(g ** 2) for g in grads.values())) if total > max_norm: scale = max_norm / (total + 1e-6) grads = {k: g * scale for k, g in grads.items()} return grads ``` The diagnostic: **print gradient norms during training.** Norms trending toward `1e-8` mean vanishing; norms exploding to `1e5` or producing `NaN` mean the opposite. Both are visible in seconds and invisible if you only watch the loss. ##### Regularization Deep networks have enormous capacity and will memorize training data given the chance. **Dropout** randomly zeroes a fraction of activations during training, forcing the network to build redundant representations rather than depending on any single unit: ```python def dropout(a, rate=0.5, training=True): if not training or rate == 0: return a, None mask = (np.random.rand(*a.shape) > rate) / (1 - rate) # inverted dropout return a * mask, mask ``` Dividing by `(1 - rate)` is **inverted dropout**: it scales the surviving activations up during training so that no adjustment is needed at inference. **Dropout must be disabled at inference** — a live model producing different predictions for identical input is a genuine and confusing bug. Typical rates are 0.2–0.5 for hidden layers, lower for inputs, and none in the output layer. **Weight decay (L2)** penalizes large weights, encouraging simpler functions: ```python # Add to the gradient: ∂/∂W of (λ/2)·||W||² = λW grads["W1"] += weight_decay * net.W1 ``` Note that **AdamW** implements weight decay correctly for adaptive optimizers, decoupling it from the gradient scaling — with plain Adam, L2 regularization interacts badly with the per-parameter scaling. **Early stopping** is the simplest and often the most effective: monitor validation loss and stop when it stops improving, keeping the best checkpoint. ##### Batch normalization Batch norm normalizes each layer's pre-activation values across the batch, then applies a learned scale and shift: ```python class BatchNorm: def __init__(self, dim, momentum=0.9, eps=1e-5): self.gamma, self.beta = np.ones(dim), np.zeros(dim) # learned self.running_mean, self.running_var = np.zeros(dim), np.ones(dim) self.momentum, self.eps = momentum, eps def forward(self, z, training=True): if training: mu, var = z.mean(axis=0), z.var(axis=0) # Track running statistics for inference self.running_mean = self.momentum * self.running_mean + (1 - self.momentum) * mu self.running_var = self.momentum * self.running_var + (1 - self.momentum) * var else: mu, var = self.running_mean, self.running_var # use stored stats z_norm = (z - mu) / np.sqrt(var + self.eps) return self.gamma * z_norm + self.beta ``` The benefits are substantial: faster convergence, tolerance of higher learning rates, reduced sensitivity to initialization, and a mild regularizing effect from batch noise. The critical implementation detail is the **train/inference distinction**. During training it uses batch statistics; at inference it must use the running averages, because a single-sample batch has zero variance. Forgetting to switch modes is among the most common deep learning bugs, and it produces predictions that vary with batch composition. For small batches or sequence models, **layer normalization** (normalizing across features rather than across the batch) is preferred — it is what transformers use. ##### Learning rate scheduling A fixed learning rate is a compromise: large enough for early progress is too large for final convergence. ```python def step_decay(epoch, initial=0.01, drop=0.5, every=20): return initial * (drop ** (epoch // every)) def cosine_annealing(epoch, total, initial=0.01, min_lr=1e-6): return min_lr + 0.5 * (initial - min_lr) * (1 + np.cos(np.pi * epoch / total)) def warmup_then_cosine(step, warmup_steps, total_steps, peak=0.001): if step < warmup_steps: return peak * step / warmup_steps # linear warmup progress = (step - warmup_steps) / (total_steps - warmup_steps) return 0.5 * peak * (1 + np.cos(np.pi * progress)) ``` **Warmup followed by cosine decay** is the modern default, particularly for transformers. Warmup prevents the large, unstable updates that occur when Adam's moment estimates are still unreliable in the first few hundred steps; cosine decay then anneals smoothly to near zero for precise final convergence. `ReduceLROnPlateau` — halving the rate whenever validation loss stalls — is a simple, effective alternative that requires no schedule design. ```mermaid flowchart TD A[Loss not decreasing] --> B{Check gradient norms} B -->|near 1e-8| C[VANISHING
ReLU, He init, BatchNorm,
residual connections] B -->|huge or NaN| D[EXPLODING
gradient clipping,
lower LR] B -->|normal| E{Train loss falling,
val loss rising?} E -->|yes| F[OVERFITTING
dropout, weight decay,
early stopping, more data] E -->|no, both flat| G[UNDERFITTING
more capacity, higher LR,
train longer, better features] C --> H[Retrain and watch
the loss curve] D --> H F --> H G --> H ``` ##### A complete training loop ```python def train(net, X_train, y_train, X_val, y_val, epochs=100, batch_size=32, lr=0.001, weight_decay=1e-4, patience=10): params = {"W1": net.W1, "b1": net.b1, "W2": net.W2, "b2": net.b2} optimizer = Adam(params, lr=lr) best_val, best_weights, wait = np.inf, None, 0 history = {"train": [], "val": []} for epoch in range(epochs): # Shuffle each epoch so batches differ idx = np.random.permutation(len(X_train)) X_shuffled, y_shuffled = X_train[idx], y_train[idx] for i in range(0, len(X_train), batch_size): Xb, yb = X_shuffled[i:i+batch_size], y_shuffled[i:i+batch_size] net.forward(Xb) grads = net.backward(yb) grads["W1"] += weight_decay * net.W1 # L2 grads["W2"] += weight_decay * net.W2 grads = clip_gradients(grads, max_norm=5.0) optimizer.step(params, grads) train_loss = bce(y_train, net.forward(X_train)) val_loss = bce(y_val, net.forward(X_val)) history["train"].append(train_loss) history["val"].append(val_loss) if val_loss < best_val - 1e-4: # early stopping best_val, wait = val_loss, 0 best_weights = {k: v.copy() for k, v in params.items()} else: wait += 1 if wait >= patience: print(f"Early stopping at epoch {epoch}, best val {best_val:.4f}") break for k, v in best_weights.items(): # restore the best params[k][:] = v return history ``` Note the shape: shuffle, iterate minibatches, forward, backward, regularize, clip, step, then evaluate and check for early stopping. **Every training loop you write in PyTorch will have this structure** — the framework computes gradients for you, but the skeleton is identical. ##### Common mistakes - **Sigmoid in deep hidden layers** — the twelve-hour flat loss. - **Learning rate too high** (`NaN` loss) or too low (no movement). Always check first. - **Forgetting to zero gradients** between steps — in PyTorch this means a missing `optimizer.zero_grad()`, and gradients accumulate silently. - **Dropout or batch norm left active at inference**, giving nondeterministic predictions. - **Not shuffling** between epochs, so the model sees the same batch composition every time. - **Unnormalized inputs**, which makes optimization badly conditioned. - **No gradient clipping** on recurrent or very deep networks. - **Never plotting the loss curve**, which diagnoses almost everything. - **Batch size 1** — extremely noisy gradients and no hardware parallelism. - **Skipping gradient checking** on a from-scratch implementation, then debugging blind. ##### Your hands-on tie-in The practical task: extend your from-scratch network to implement **backpropagation**, train it on a small dataset, and **watch the loss decrease**. Run gradient checking first — if your analytic and numerical gradients disagree, everything downstream is meaningless, and finding that out in two minutes beats debugging a training loop for an hour. The mini project is a **configurable NumPy trainer** supporting different **optimizers and regularization**, comparing their convergence. Plot SGD, SGD+momentum and Adam on the same loss curve — Adam will typically drop fastest early, momentum will catch up, and plain SGD will trail. Then add dropout and weight decay and watch the train/validation gap narrow. Those two figures make the whole article concrete. For the assignment, **explain the vanishing gradient problem and two techniques that mitigate it**. Show the arithmetic — `0.25¹⁰ ≈ 1e-6` versus `1.0¹⁰ = 1` — because the exponential collapse is the entire explanation. For mitigations, ReLU (derivative of 1 preserves gradient magnitude) and residual connections (a direct additive path backwards) are the strongest pair; batch normalization and careful initialization are also defensible. ##### Key takeaways - Backpropagation applies the chain rule backwards, computing every gradient in one pass by reusing stored forward-pass values — verify your implementation with gradient checking. - Adam with `lr=0.001` is the robust default; momentum carries updates through plateaus, and adaptive per-parameter rates handle badly-scaled problems. - Vanishing gradients come from multiplying small derivatives through depth — ReLU, He initialization, batch norm and residual connections are the fixes; clip gradients for the exploding case. - Dropout, weight decay and early stopping are the core regularizers, and dropout and batch norm must behave differently at inference. - Use warmup plus cosine decay for the learning rate, and plot the loss curve every time — it diagnoses vanishing gradients, overfitting and underfitting at a glance.
